summary: Three related topics past the standard lung-protective bundle. APRV setup varies more across centers than any other mode. Aggressive maximal recruitment (ART: PEEP 45, peak 60) caused harm — a moderate staircase maneuver plus a decremental PEEP trial is a different thing. In the routine surgical patient, low tidal volume does the work; added PEEP/recruitment mostly adds hemodynamic cost.
whyThisMatters: The interventions past the lung-protective bundle are where enthusiasm outran evidence: maximal recruitment (ART) killed patients, APRV is set up differently at every center, and routine intraoperative PEEP mostly buys hemodynamic cost for no benefit. Knowing where the line is matters more than knowing the maneuvers.
clinicalTakeaway:
In established ARDS, low tidal volume and a titrated PEEP do the work; reserve a moderate staircase recruitment plus a decremental PEEP trial for refractory hypoxemia, and avoid the ART-style maximal maneuver. Use APRV only if the team runs it routinely.

In the routine surgical patient, low tidal volume is enough — don't add PEEP or recruitment reflexively.

For refractory hypoxemia despite all of this:
- prone EARLY in moderate-severe ARDS (P/F ≤150) rather than as a last resort
- reserve neuromuscular blockade for dyssynchrony/proning rather than a routine continuous infusion
- treat inhaled nitric oxide as a temporizing bridge, not a therapy with a mortality benefit

rows: P high
Set to the Pplat from the prior conventional mode; do not exceed 30 cmH₂O
P low

Commonly 0 — this does NOT create zero PEEP: the release time is too brief for full emptying, so meaningful intrinsic PEEP persists. Raising P low above 0 unpredictably changes both intrinsic PEEP and delivered VT
T high
4–6 s with reasonably preserved lungs; a longer T high improves oxygenation
T low
The most consequential and least standardized — commonly set to terminate the release at 50–75% of the peak expiratory flow, targeting ~ 10–14 releases/min

items: Hypoxemia: raise P high and/or T high (and FiO₂) first.
Hypercapnia: shorten T high to increase release frequency, or lighten sedation to allow more spontaneous breathing — spontaneous effort is central to how APRV works, not incidental.

Evidence (2026 meta-analysis, 9 studies, ~1900 patients): APRV/BiVent improved oxygenation and ventilator-free days vs conventional ventilation, with no mortality benefit. Treat any single center's protocol as one implementation among several.

rows: Staircase recruitment
Step PEEP up in stages (e.g. 4→10 for a few breaths, 10→15, 15→20 held longer), peak capped ~ 40–50 cmH₂O — well below ART's 60
Decremental PEEP trial
After the maneuver, step PEEP down (e.g. by 2 every few minutes) watching oxygenation and compliance; the lowest PEEP before benefit is lost, plus a small margin, is the working PEEP

body.text: ART's harm signal was about the technique and magnitude (sustained 45–60 cmH₂O), not the concept of recruitment. Still: abort any maneuver for hypotension or new desaturation, avoid it in hypovolemia / right-heart failure / a known bronchopleural fistula, and only recruit lungs that are recruitable (diffuse ARDS, early, high P/F response).

rows: IMPROVE (NEJM 2013)
Major abdominal surgery — VT 6–8 mL/kg PBW + PEEP 6–8 + recruitment q30min vs VT 10–12, no PEEP: the protective strategy reduced major pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications
PROVHILO (Lancet 2014)

Both arms already low-VT — high PEEP (12) + recruitment vs low PEEP (≤ 2), no recruitment: no difference in pulmonary complications; the high-PEEP arm had more intraoperative hypotension and vasopressor use

body.text: Read together: the low tidal volume is doing the real work. In the routine open-abdominal population, PEEP and recruitment added on top add hemodynamic cost without a demonstrated benefit — a mirror of the ART pattern in a lower-acuity population. Later trials (PROBESE in obesity, iPROVE-OLV in one-lung ventilation) suggest PEEP/recruitment may still matter in specific subgroups; that is unsettled.

When lung-protective ventilation plus a reasonable PEEP/recruitment strategy still leaves a patient severely hypoxemic, three further interventions are commonly reached for — but they carry very different evidence bases and should not be treated as interchangeable 'more rescue' options.

rows: Prone positioning

PROSEVA (NEJM 2013): moderate-severe ARDS (P/F ≤ 150), prone ≥16 h/day, started EARLY — 28-day mortality 16% prone vs 32.8% supine, one of the largest mortality effects of any ARDS intervention studied, bigger than lung-protective ventilation itself produced in its own original trials

First-line rescue, not a last resort — apply EARLY in moderate-severe ARDS (P/F ≤150) rather than waiting until every other option is exhausted. Needs a protocolized team (pressure injury prevention, ETT/line security, a plan for the patient developing an emergency while prone).
Neuromuscular blockade (paralysis)

ROSE (NEJM 2019): continuous 48-hour cisatracurium infusion with deep sedation was NOT superior to as-needed NMB with lighter sedation in moderate-severe ARDS, and the continuous-infusion arm trended toward more cardiovascular adverse events

Don't reflexively start a continuous 48-hour paralytic infusion as a default early-ARDS strategy (this reversed earlier, smaller-trial-driven practice). Reserve NMB for patient-ventilator dyssynchrony, refractory hypoxemia, or during proning itself, using it as-needed rather than as a fixed continuous infusion.
Inhaled nitric oxide (or inhaled epoprostenol)

Multiple trials/meta-analyzes (Cochrane 2016 and subsequent): reliably improves oxygenation transiently, but has never demonstrated a mortality benefit and carries a signal for renal impairment with prolonged use

Use as a temporizing BRIDGE for severe, refractory hypoxemia (e.g. while arranging proning, ECMO transfer, or another definitive step) — not as a routine ARDS therapy, and be honest that it's buying time/oxygenation numbers rather than changing the outcome trajectory on its own.

body.text: Rough priority order for genuinely refractory hypoxemia: optimize lung-protective ventilation and PEEP first, prone EARLY if P/F ≤150 (don't save it for last), reserve neuromuscular blockade for dyssynchrony/proning/persistent refractory hypoxemia rather than routine continuous use, and treat inhaled pulmonary vasodilators as a bridge — with ECMO as the next escalation if all of this is failing (see ECMO & Advanced Circulatory Support).
